items.title: Jester Lands in Court: Florida Woman Accused of Stealing Properties With Forged Deeds
items.description: A Florida woman has been accused of perpetrating a brazen deed fraud scam and illicitly transferred ownership of three properties in a scheme to fund her lavish lifestyle. Melissa Jester , 41, of Bunnell, FL , is facing criminal charges after authorities say she forged a property owner's signature on deeds, transferred the land to a company she controlled, and pocketed the proceeds from one of the sales. She was arrested Nov. 6. The victim, who owned three vacant lots in Florida for nearly two decades, recently discovered that the properties were transferred out of her name without her knowledge—and that one had been sold for nearly $30,000, according to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office . The victim contacted the authorities on Aug. 27 and said she had never authorized the sale or transfer of the properties. The three lots are located in the coastal city of Palm Coast, about 30 miles north of Daytona Beach. An investigation was launched, and detectives uncovered what they described as a paper trail of forged documents , suspicious financial transactions, and a property sale that ultimately helped lead them to Jester . Detectives traced a trail of forged documents and fraudulent financial transactions to Jester. According to investigators, paperwork transferring ownership of all three lots to Florida Ohana Homes LLC, a company owned by Jester, was mailed to the Flagler County Clerk of Courts on June 29, 2026. The paperwork appeared to have the property owner's signature on it. It was forged, investigators say. Jester took further steps to hide her involvement by purchasing a money order on June 18 to pay the filing fees for the property under a different name, according to the affidavit. The money order was purchased at the Amscot location on Palm Coast Parkway. The transaction did not require identification. But the alleged scheme did not end there. According to the Flagler County Sheriff’s Office, Jester, acting as managing member of Florida Ohana Homes LLC, then sold one of the stolen lots for $29,970 to an unsuspecting buyer on Sept. 10. Surveillance video from the UPS Store on Belle Terre Parkway showed Jester signing the warranty deed and having it notarized. The money was transferred to the Bank of America account for Florida Ohana Homes LLC. Authorities also allege that Jester transferred $8,000 from the business account into her personal account at VyStar Credit Union, where the money was spent on hotel stays and purchases throughout Flagler County. By following the financial transactions, detectives were able to trace the money and recover a substantial portion of the proceeds from the alleged illicit sale. More than $14,000 was seized from the company's Bank of America account and another $6,000 from Jester's personal credit union account. A total of $20,000 was recovered. On Nov. 6, deputies located Jester driving in Bunnell, FL, and arrested her on charges of grand theft and obtaining property valued between $20,000 and $50,000 by swindle. She is being held at the Sheriff Perry Hall Inmate Detention Facility on a $45,000 bond. Flagler County Sheriff Rick Staly said the case stood out because, unlike many property fraud schemes involving suspects operating from distant locations, the alleged perpetrator lived nearby and conducted the transaction in person. “Most of the deed fraud we see is run by scammers hiding in another state or another country. This one lived in Bunnell and signed the closing papers in front of a security camera in Palm Coast,” Sheriff Staly said. “Our detectives followed the trail of forgeries and money and recovered most of it for the victim.” Get real estate news in your inbox Sign up now

items.title: This U.S. Marine Is Building a Wearable Health Tracker Designed for Veterans
items.description: Live Poll In 2010, United States Marine Devin Harris was wounded on the battlefield in Afghanistan. His courage earned him a Purple Heart. But he also returned home with a collection of different devices, trackers, and monitors to keep an eye on his progress as he recovered from his injuries. After he was healed up and he left the armed forces, a business idea started to form. He noticed that his fellow veterans were not getting the adequate support they needed from Veterans Affairs hospitals or private healthcare. So, he started thinking about how he could leverage the data that wearable health trackers—such as the Apple Watch, FitBit, or Oura Ring—collect to identify physical and mental health crises. Ultimately, the goal is to intervene before a veteran goes through a health crisis. To turn the thesis into a business, Harris teamed up with Trey Bowles and Ryan Brown of 1845 Ventures, to found Optimus OS. The company's flagship product is Cadence, a wristband tracker about the size of a watch designed for veterans. It launches this week. Introducing: The POWER 50 Our new program spotlights North Texas executives under 50 shaping the region’s future. Nominations are open through Nov. 13. Learn More The Cadence band tracks the wearer's biometrics to try to prevent health issues common in veterans, like PTSD and traumatic brain injuries. "We're focusing on looking at veterans holistically day-to-day, on a preventative basis," Harris said. The band monitors everything from heart rate to sleep quality to caloric output to stress markers. Every data point was identified as an indicator for problems that occur at higher rates in veterans, like cardiovascular problems, post-traumatic stress disorder, and traumatic brain injuries. Harris said Optimus helps with what he calls the "continuum of care" for veterans: the community and medical support that many former service members need once they return to civilian life. The data the band collects can inform medical professionals on what may be the issue, and partnerships with veteran service organizations help keep members from becoming isolated. "It's really good for the individual patient, the veteran, because they're more informed and they're building that kind of community," he said. "I've lost, unfortunately, way too many friends who didn't have that continuum of care." The band uses technology designed by Sensor Bio, a biometrics platform based in Austin. Harris said Optimus is partnering with other groups that specialize in issues like PTSD to help identify crisis indicators in the wearer. "It's not going to be able to diagnose, but it can give precursors that help practitioners make more informed choices," Harris said. Optimus has already partnered with the California chapter of the Military Order of the Purple Heart, of which Harris is a member. He said the partnerships will have a "buy one, get one" model where a percentage of sales benefit veteran support organizations. He's also looking at working with companies like USAA that hire high numbers of veterans, plus the Department of Defense, to provide Optimus bands to employees. First responders are also part of the target demographic for Optimus, Harris said, since they face many of the same health risks. Civilians will also be able to purchase the band once it's commercially available. The plan now, Harris said, is to launch the bands with partners this week and begin commercial programs in December, with order fulfillment starting in January. Then he'll aim for the VA and DoD. "A guiding factor for me is how I can take patients, connect them with clinicians, and then use data to fill gaps and needs," Harris said. "I like building things with the mission of being able to connect veterans to better forms of care." items.title: Housing demand shows signs of stabilizing. Does your market?
items.description: Lower mortgage rates are helping stabilize housing demand even as inventory has declined, according to Logan Mohtashami's latest Housing Market Tracker . But a national housing demand signal doesn't mean every local market is following. And even within the same metro area, buyer activity can tell very different stories. The Deltona–Daytona Beach–Ormond Beach metro area in Florida offers a useful example. New pending listings across the metro area increased 20.2% year over year in October, according to HousingWire Data . A closer look at individual cities, however, reveals that the improvement was far from uniform. One metro, different patterns of buyer activity In Ormond Beach, Fla., new pending listings increased 116.7% year over year in October, rising from 72 in 2025 to 156 in 2026. Nearby Port Orange recorded an 80% increase, while Daytona Beach saw a 63.2% gain. But Deltona, one of the cities that gives the metro area its name, experienced a 24.3% decline. New pending listings fell from 136 to 103. New Smyrna Beach also recorded a decline of 25.3%. Different patterns of buyer activity. This chart compares weekly new pending listings in Ormond Beach and Deltona over the past six months. While both cities experience fluctuations in weekly activity, their October year-over-year trends tell different stories. Adjust the date range or select YoY to explore how each city's activity compares with its historical performance. For housing professionals, the distinction matters. A regional market can be gaining momentum while individual communities within it are moving in the opposite direction. Seasonality doesn't look the same everywhere Fall typically brings a slowdown in housing activity, but the timing and magnitude can vary significantly by market. That's why a change in new pending listings needs seasonal context. Consider the average weekly new pending listings in three Volusia County cities between September and October 2026: Ormond Beach: Increased from 28 to 31.2 per week, up 11.4% . Port Orange: Increased from 16.3 to 19.8 per week, up 21.5% . Deltona: Declined from 26 to 20.6 per week, down 20.8% . Historical trends add another layer. Ormond Beach also experienced an increase in average weekly new pending listings between September and October in 2025, but the increase was smaller. Deltona experienced an increase during that period in 2025 before reversing direction this year. The lesson isn't that one city is stronger than another. It's that seasonal changes can play out differently even in neighboring communities. A decline in new pending listings may be consistent with a market's typical seasonal pattern. A smaller-than-usual decline could signal improving momentum. And an increase in activity deserves a closer look to determine whether it represents a sustained shift or a short-term fluctuation. What to watch in your own market The Florida example raises a useful question: Are changes in buyer activity consistent across the communities you serve, or is the broader market trend masking important differences? Four metrics can help you recognize changes, understand what they might signal and put that information to work. 1. New pending listings: Is buyer activity gaining momentum? What to watch: Compare new pending listings with the same period last year and track changes over several consecutive weeks. Look for activity that differs from the market's typical seasonal pattern. What it could mean: Sustained increases may indicate strengthening buyer activity, while declines can signal weakening demand. A smaller-than-usual seasonal decline may also be an early sign of stabilization. How to use it: Identify communities where buyer activity is changing. Agents can use that information to set expectations with buyers and sellers, while loan officers can help referral partners understand where transaction opportunities may be improving. 2. New listings: Is supply keeping pace with demand? What to watch: Compare the number of new listings entering the market with new pending listings. Is the gap between them widening or narrowing? What it could mean: When new pending activity increases relative to new listings, buyers may be absorbing a greater share of incoming supply. When new listings grow faster than new pending activity, more homes may be competing for buyers' attention. How to use it: Evaluate whether buyers are likely to encounter more competition or more choices. For agents, that can inform pricing and offer strategies. For lending teams, it can help identify markets where purchase activity may be gaining momentum relative to available opportunities. 3. Price reductions: Are seller expectations adjusting? What to watch: Track the share of active listings with price reductions and whether that share is rising or falling over several weeks. What it could mean: A rising share may suggest sellers are having difficulty attracting buyers at their initial asking prices. A declining share could indicate better alignment between pricing and buyer expectations, although changes in listing mix and seasonality can also influence the metric. How to use it: Bring evidence into pricing conversations rather than relying solely on recent comparable sales. Loan officers can use the same information to help referral partners understand negotiating conditions and where pricing expectations may be changing. 4. Days on market: Is the pace of the market changing? What to watch: Compare median days on market with recent weeks and the same period last year. Look for whether homes are spending more or less time on the market. What it could mean: Shorter marketing times alongside stronger new pending activity may reinforce evidence of improving demand. Longer marketing times, particularly when new pending activity is declining, may indicate that buyers are becoming more selective or that listings are taking longer to find the right price. items.title: Winning in a buyer’s market
items.description: As we head into the end of the year, we are at a truly magical moment for buyers across much of America. Buyers have more houses to choose from, along with the ability to inspect the property, negotiate repairs and make homeownership more affordable . It is something buyers have been wanting for years, but where are all the buyers? Pending sales were recently recorded as the lowest since they started tracking pending sales! Currently, many buyers are holding back for three main reasons. As a mortgage lender or real estate agent, knowing these reasons and how to solve them is the key to helping your buyers win right now. Would I recommend waiting for lower rates? Absolutely not; the lower the rates, the more competition, and it is the lack of competition where true opportunity lies. Reason 1: Rates are high Ask the seller to pay to buy down the mortgage rate . I like a permanent buydown as it gives certainty for the long run. Many buyers can afford the house when the rate starts at 6%, so use a seller buydown to get there. Reason 2: The price is too high Offer less. Many buyers do not know that you can offer less. They are waiting for the seller to drop the price when, in reality, they should just write an offer now with what they want to pay. It is up to the seller to say yes or no. Whether the seller agrees depends on their financial situation and their motivation to sell. I have chatted with clients who want the house, but not at the current price and are afraid to offer $10,000 less. To me, that's a missed opportunity. The seller could be sitting on the other side praying they get an offer. Write the offer. Reason 3: I don’t have enough saved for closing costs Did you know many buyers don't realize they can ask the seller to pay for closing costs? Over 42% of recent sales have seller concessions, but many buyers still do not know you can ask for this. You could have a buyer you talked to last year who was in a seller's market, who is saving away, who does not even know that their market is now a buyer's market. This is your opportunity as a real estate professional to help them get home. Ask the seller to pay their closing costs and help them get home for the Holidays. As I type this, we have buyers across the country negotiating for lower sales prices, closing costs and rate buydown covered by the seller. Does every seller say yes? No, but that is the beauty of the buyer's market; there are so many sellers to choose from. There is tremendous opportunity in the market right now for buyers to win. Help them seize it. items.title: Third spaces perform a star turn in this new Florida master plan
items.description: In a crowded, competitive and bumpy market, residential developers and builders do their best to stand out in a sea of sameness. Some bet that they'll seize a competitive edge by leaning into walkable communities with "third spaces," ones where residents can easily connect with one another and feel a sense of belonging. Wyld Oaks, an upcoming mixed-use community near Orlando, Florida , where construction is now underway, will put that thesis to the test. In October, Hathaway Development became the first developer to begin horizontal construction at Wyld Oaks , where it is building 325 apartment units. That's for starters. Once fully built out, the community is expected to have 6,000 multifamily units and a small adjoining single-family portion with fewer than 100 homes. Residential, mind you, is only part of the plan. Wyld Oaks is designed around a walkable main street anchored by a large park and 300,000 square feet of retail space. Elsewhere in the community, the master plan calls for two hotels, a medical campus, 1.5 million square feet of industrial and distribution space, multiple other parks, an outdoor concert venue and a gas station. For Wyld Oaks master developer Joseph Beninati, the goal is to create a walkable, mixed-use community that functions like a complete neighborhood, with daily needs all within walking or biking distance. “Could you take your car? Of course you can,” Beninati said in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “But the option to walk is going to be there.” With walkability at its core, Wyld Oaks stands apart from the overwhelming majority of new suburban development in the region, which is largely car-centric. Getting the project off the ground has been difficult, however. The original multifamily development, which only just broke ground, was slated to begin in late 2024 or early 2025. The delay resulted from a challenging local multifamily capital environment that has plagued many other Sun Belt markets. A main street with 300,000 square feet of retail and a large green space will anchor Wyld Oaks. Despite this growth, and the rapid growth of adjacent communities, there remain relatively few walkable, mixed-use neighborhoods for residents and visitors alike. This need in the market was among the top considerations for Wyld Oaks, which was designed with walkability, livability and community in mind. “It all starts with density, and trail systems and parks, and having everything closer to one another as opposed to further apart. We have multifamily, and we're working on retail, food and beverage, coffee stores and grocery stores, all within walking distance,” Beninati said. “Run the list. [Residents] need fitness. They need healthcare. They need a convenience store and daily conveniences, dry cleaning, hair salons and barber shops.” All of the commercial uses designed within easy walking distances in the community will work together to keep residents in the neighborhood, bring in employees to work at the industrial park and various businesses and draw in visitors to enjoy the local shops, restaurants and parks. Once fully built out, Beninati expects, or at least hopes, that Wyld Oaks will become a top-tier regional destination. “Economic activity begets economic activity. If you’re bringing your kids to the dentist, that allows you to also maybe do a little grocery shopping. Or if you're going to work out and you're with some friends, maybe you're going to go out and have a drink or supper together. When everything is in one place, it allows that to happen,” Beninati explained. Beninati envisions a neighborhood where residents can get outdoors and meet one another, whether at local parks, restaurants, the community’s future farmers market or other events. For visitors, he wants a community that is memorable and draws people back in. “For me, some of the softer things would be, are prom pictures getting taken and wedding pictures getting taken there? Or is it a meaningful place that the community rallies around? Is there a Christmas tree, and is there going to be a Halloween event for the kids? Things like that are what make a community something that is memorable,” he said. items.title: 3 ways lenders can keep a divorce refinance on track
items.description: 3 ways lenders can keep a divorce refinance on track By Eric Bernstein Published November 11, 2026, 2:40 p.m. EST 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Earlier this year, a borrower came to us with a signed settlement requiring her to pay her former husband $210,000 for his half of the equity in their home, with 90 days to refinance. The house had nearly doubled in value over 14 years. On her income alone, before the child support in the agreement had started arriving, she qualified for about $70,000 less than she owed. Processing Content More borrowers are landing in her position as equity builds up in homes people hold for longer. Mortgaged homeowners held an average of roughly $310,000 in equity in the second quarter, according to Cotality , and sellers in the National Association of Realtors' latest profile had owned their homes for a record median of 11 years. That appreciation sets the size of the check one spouse writes the other, and the figure is usually agreed before a lender has seen any numbers. Whether the spouse who stays can keep the house depends on three things a lender controls: how that borrower is qualified, how early the preapproval comes, and how the loan is classified. Qualify the borrower who's staying, not the household The departing spouse's share becomes new debt for the spouse who stays. It sits on top of whatever it takes to retire the joint mortgage and is underwritten against one person's income and obligations. A car loan and credit card balances that two salaries handled comfortably now weigh on a single income in the debt-to-income calculation. Support income is where loan officers and borrowers most often get caught out. Fannie Mae counts alimony or child support only after six months of documented receipt , with evidence it will continue for at least three years. It won't consider proposed or voluntary payments at all without an agreement that specifies them. A borrower relying on support to carry their ratios can reach the refinance deadline before that income is usable. A borrower who pays support loses qualifying capacity from the first month. Get the preapproval in before the buyout figure is final Most of the divorce refinances I've watched fall apart were effectively decided before an application existed. The couple settles on a figure, a deadline goes into the decree, and the spouse keeping the house assumes financing will follow. When it doesn't, they either reopen the agreement or sell the home they were both trying to protect. Meanwhile, the departing spouse stays on a joint loan for a house they no longer live in. Lenders can change that only by getting involved once one spouse has decided to keep the home. At that point, the work is a full preapproval on the individual borrower's profile, along with a frank conversation about the monthly payment they can live with, which is often lower than what they qualify for. How to divide what they own is the couple's decision. Our job is to show what that division has to fit within while there's still time to shape the terms. Sometimes that means a parent joining as a non-occupant co-borrower. In other cases, the couple offsets part of the house against retirement accounts so less cash changes hands at closing, or times the refinance so support income has the history it needs. For originators wondering how to reach these borrowers, rate-driven marketing misses the moment entirely. What gets attention is an offer to show what keeping the house would cost, including the new payment and whether support income will count by the deadline. Timing is the whole pitch. Structure the buyout so it funds the full share Fannie Mae treats a buyout of a co-owner under a written agreement as a limited cash-out refinance , provided the property was jointly owned for at least 12 months before the new loan funds. File the same transaction as a standard cash-out refinance, and it runs into a lower loan-to-value ceiling and heavier pricing adjustments, which can shrink the buyout the borrower can fund. The conditions need managing early. Every party has to sign an agreement setting out how the proceeds will be distributed, and the spouse keeping the home can't receive any of the cash. Structured correctly, a single closing pays off the joint mortgage, releases the departing spouse from it and delivers their share. Where lenders earn their place More divorcing borrowers will arrive with large sums at stake as people hold homes longer and values keep climbing underneath them. The deals that collapse usually do so for reasons a lender could have flagged months earlier, such as a buyout figure set without any financing input or a loan filed under the wrong category. Originators who make themselves available when the decision to keep the house is made, rather than when the decree is final, give these borrowers a realistic chance of staying in their homes.
